messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had been a social worker for over two decades, dedicating his life to helping others. But it was a traumatic event from his past that now threatened to unravel everything he had worked for. Five years ago, while attending a conference in another city, Kofi was sexually assaulted by an acquaintance. The details of the attack were forever seared into his mind: the feeling of being trapped, the helplessness, and the shame. As memories of that night resurfaced, Kofi would often become overwhelmed with terror, reliving the same fear he felt during the assault. When this happened, he found himself ruminating about how to get even with his assailant, fantasizing about revenge as a way to regain control. He also tried to push these thoughts out of his mind, attempting to suppress them with varying degrees of success. But the more he pushed, the more they seemed to linger. The shame associated with the memory was another constant companion for Kofi. When recalling the event, he couldn't shake off the feeling that it was somehow his fault, that he should have been able to prevent it. This self-blame made it even harder for him to open up about what happened, and as a result, he struggled to find words to describe the experience. As Kofi navigated his daily life, these memories continued to shape his perceptions of the world around him. He started to notice potential threats everywhere – every stranger on the street became a possible assailant, every unfamiliar place a potential trap. When walking home from work, he frequently looked over his shoulder, checking if someone was following him. His avoidance of enclosed or confined spaces grew more pronounced, and even simple tasks like grocery shopping became daunting ordeals. When delays occurred in his daily routine – whether it was a traffic jam or a delayed appointment – Kofi's mind would immediately jump to the worst-case scenario: something bad is happening, he thought, my assailant has found me. This hypervigilance had become so ingrained that even small setbacks triggered a cascade of catastrophic thinking. Kofi's avoidance behaviors had also started to affect his work as a social worker. He began turning down cases involving victims of assault or abuse, unable to confront the memories and emotions these situations stirred up in him. His colleagues noticed a change in him – he was more withdrawn, less confident in his abilities – but Kofi couldn't explain what was happening. As the months went by, Kofi's relationships suffered too. His wife grew increasingly frustrated with his moodiness, his inability to connect on an intimate level. She sensed that something was wrong, but Kofi pushed her away, ashamed of his weakness. He knew he needed help but felt trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance. One evening, as he was walking home from work, Kofi caught himself checking behind him for the umpteenth time. In that moment, he realized how exhausting this constant hypervigilance had become. The memories still lingered, the shame still burned, but something inside him shifted – a spark of recognition that it was time to confront these demons head-on, rather than trying to outrun them forever. It was this glimmer of awareness that finally led Kofi to seek help, driven by a desire to break free from the suffocating grip of his memories and reclaim control over his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, ready to confront the darkness within him, Kofi felt a flicker of hope – maybe, just maybe, he could learn to live with these memories without being consumed by them.
